title: Polynomial-time weighted falsifiability of unambiguous DNFs
formal:
Does there exist one uniform deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the total binary input length, that decides weighted falsifiability for every unambiguous DNF? Given
\[F=\bigvee_{j=1}^{m}T_j,\qquad w_1,\ldots,w_n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,\]
it must decide whether
\[\exists a\in\{0,1\}^{n}:\qquad F(a)=0\quad\land\quad\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i a_i\ge t.\]
Each term \(T_j\) is explicitly listed, and the weights and threshold are binary integers. Unambiguity means that no assignment satisfies two distinct term occurrences. The threshold is “at least,” not exact equality.
definitions:
An instance lists integers \(n,m\ge0\), a DNF formula on \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), one nonnegative weight for each of the \(n\) variables, and a signed integer threshold. A literal is \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\). Each term \(T_j\) is a finite list of literals interpreted as their conjunction, and \(F\) is the disjunction of the terms. The empty term is true; a DNF with no terms is false. Repeating a literal within a term has no effect, and a term containing both signs of a variable is always false. Such contradictory terms may be deleted without changing the function or its unambiguity.

A Boolean assignment \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) gives each variable a bit; a positive literal is true when the bit is 1 and a negative literal when it is 0. Formally, unambiguity is
\[\forall a\in\{0,1\}^{n},\qquad |\{j:T_j(a)=1\}|\le1.\]
For consistent terms, this is equivalent to every pair containing opposite signs of some common variable. Thus unambiguity can be checked in polynomial time from the explicit lists. Duplicate consistent term occurrences violate the condition. Unused variables remain part of the assignment and contribute their weights.

Use a fixed explicitly delimited binary encoding of the lists: variable indices, list lengths and nonnegative integers are binary, literal signs and the threshold sign are explicit, and every list entry is written in full. Let \(L\) be the total number of bits, including the formula, all weights and the threshold. The question concerns a deterministic multitape Turing machine with running time at most \(C(L+1)^d\) for fixed constants \(C,d\), on all inputs. It has no randomness, oracle, advice or unit-cost arithmetic on arbitrarily long integers. The cost of exact integer arithmetic is included. Syntactically invalid inputs, invalid variable indices, negative weights and formulas failing unambiguity are rejected. Because validity and unambiguity are polynomial-time checkable, this total-language convention preserves the intended promised-input question.

An accepted input must have at least one falsifying assignment meeting the threshold. If \(F\) is a tautology there is no such assignment, whatever \(t\) is. With \(W=\sum_iw_i\), a threshold larger than \(W\) always gives no, and a threshold at most zero asks ordinary falsifiability. The definitions also cover \(n=0\), where there is one empty assignment and its score is zero. Weights and comparisons are exact, without rounding or error probability.

The original author phrases the optimization version as the maximum score of a falsifying assignment, with value \(-\infty\) for a tautology. Its strict comparison \(\text{score}>t\) is equivalent to \(\text{score}\ge t+1\) for integer scores. The maintained problem list uses the latter non-strict convention. The card retains its existing decision target, equivalent to polynomial-time exact optimization because finite attainable scores lie between 0 and \(W\), whose binary length is polynomial in the input size.

A pseudopolynomial algorithm has running time polynomial in \(L\) and the numerical weight sum \(W\). This can be exponential in the bit length of a binary weight and therefore is not the requested polynomial bound. Membership in P means the existence of the single uniform machine defined above. Membership in NP means that a polynomial-length binary witness can be checked by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier; this problem lies in NP because an \(n\)-bit assignment is such a witness.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation that the defined language is in P. A positive answer must provide one deterministic algorithm and prove exact correctness and a running time polynomial in the full binary input length, including arbitrarily large binary weights. A negative answer must prove that no such polynomial-time decider exists. NP-hardness alone supplies a negative conclusion only under the additional assumption \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\); an assumption-dependent conclusion is not an unconditional refutation of this card. A pseudopolynomial algorithm, an unweighted algorithm, hardness without the unambiguity condition or hardness for exact-score equality does not settle this target. The decision and time guarantees are exact; numerical acceptance tolerance does not apply.
why: The problem isolates whether a representation with easy exact counting also supports optimization over its complement. Binary weights create a sharp distinction from the unweighted and unary cases, with consequences for the operations supported by compact Boolean representations.

importance.reason: A focused but structural tractability question connecting unambiguous representations, binary-weight optimization, and complementation. It has a clear gap between polynomial unweighted methods and an unresolved weighted case.

context_blocks.text: Unambiguity makes the satisfying sets of the individual terms disjoint. This makes the total number of satisfying assignments easy to count, and ordinary falsifiability can be decided from that count. The unresolved weighted task asks whether the complement contains a sufficiently high-scoring assignment, which is information the total count alone does not supply.

For example, \(F=(x\land y)\lor(\neg x\land z)\) is unambiguous. With weights 8, 3 and 5, the assignment \((1,0,1)\) falsifies it and has score 13. The all-ones assignment has score 16 but satisfies the formula. Thus a maximum unconstrained score need not occur outside the satisfying region.

Weighted satisfaction is polynomial-time solvable even for general DNFs, whereas weighted falsification requires all terms to fail at once. The author also notes that dropping unambiguity makes the decision problem NP-complete. These nearby easy and hard cases isolate the significance of the disjointness restriction.

For unary weights, the authors’ observations give a polynomial-time algorithm; for binary weights the same bound is only pseudopolynomial. Replacing the inequality by exact equality gives a different, NP-hard problem, so that modification cannot be used as a resolution of the stated threshold question.

The seminar report places this question among problems about compact Boolean representations used in database provenance and explanations. The issue illustrates that efficient counting and efficient optimization of falsifying assignments need not follow from the same representation properties.

The maintained list also discusses larger compiled-circuit representations. Those connections motivate the problem, while this card asks only about explicitly listed unambiguous DNFs and one additive score threshold.

sentences: The question asks whether an unambiguous DNF has a falsifying assignment whose additive integer score meets a threshold.
Every weight is encoded in binary, and the requested deterministic running time is polynomial in the entire bit representation.
Unambiguity makes the satisfying regions disjoint and ordinary falsifiability easy.
Unary-weight algorithms and hardness for exact-score equality leave the binary threshold question unsettled in the checked sources.
A complete answer must establish or refute polynomial-time decidability with the stated representation and guarantee.
